proposal.title: Trump Ends Canada Trade Talks Over Ontario’s Reagan Ad and Suggests It Was AI
proposal.description_short: Trump ended trade talks with Canada over Ontario’s Reagan ad and later suggested it may have been made using AI.
proposal.description_medium: On Oct. 23, 2025, Trump said he had terminated all trade negotiations with Canada, citing an Ontario government ad that used edited excerpts of Ronald Reagan’s 1987 remarks on tariffs. On Oct. 24, he told reporters, “I guess it was AI or something.” FactCheck.org found that the ad rearranged parts of Reagan’s address but did not change his broader anti-tariff position. Reporting documents Trump’s AI suggestion; it does not establish that AI generated the ad.
proposal.description_long: Ontario’s provincial government sponsored an advertisement using excerpts from former President Ronald Reagan’s 1987 radio address about tariffs. On Oct. 23, 2025, President Donald Trump called the ad “FAKE” on Truth Social, said it was intended to interfere with pending tariff litigation, and announced that he was terminating all trade negotiations with Canada. The Associated Press reported that the ad was sponsored by Ontario, a Canadian province, rather than Canada’s federal government. On Oct. 24, Trump told reporters, “I guess it was AI or something,” framing AI as a suggestion rather than presenting production evidence. FactCheck.org compared the ad with Reagan’s address and found that the ad rearranged portions and omitted context but did not change Reagan’s broader criticism of tariffs. The reviewed sources document Trump’s accusation and the trade-talk announcement; they do not establish that artificial intelligence generated the ad or what happened to later negotiations. This proposed event is limited to Trump’s public response and decision over the Ontario advertisement.

proposal.title: Trump Administration Suspended Most New Northern Triangle Aid and Reprogrammed FY2018 Funds
proposal.description_short: GAO found the administration suspended most new Northern Triangle aid for up to 14 months and reprogrammed about $396 million in FY2018 funds.
proposal.description_medium: On March 30, 2019, the State Department said it was carrying out President Donald Trump’s direction to end fiscal years 2017 and 2018 assistance programs for El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras, while engaging Congress. A later GAO review found the administration suspended most new State and USAID assistance to the Northern Triangle for up to 14 months and directed agencies to reprogram about $396 million, roughly 85% of planned FY2018 aid. This describes the reported policy and implementation, not a complete halt to all aid.
proposal.description_long: On March 30, 2019, the State Department said it was carrying out President Donald Trump’s direction to end fiscal year 2017 and 2018 foreign-assistance programs for El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras, known as the Northern Triangle. The department said it would engage Congress in the process. Reuters reported that the announcement followed Trump’s criticism of the three countries over migration and that a House appropriations aide estimated roughly $700 million in aid was affected; that was an estimate at the time, not a final accounting. A later Government Accountability Office review documented how the policy was implemented. State and USAID allowed previously obligated fiscal year 2017 and earlier pipeline funding to continue for ongoing projects after a review, while most new Northern Triangle assistance was suspended for up to 14 months. GAO said the administration directed the agencies to reprogram approximately $396 million, or about 85% of planned fiscal year 2018 assistance for the region. The event is therefore described as a suspension and reprogramming of aid programs, rather than a permanent end to every form of U.S. assistance to all three countries. The cited review also limits the claim: it covers the federal funding and programs it examined, not every aid channel or later policy change.

limitations: The contemporaneous $700 million figure was a House aide’s estimate; the proposal uses GAO’s later $396 million implementation figure instead.
The evidence supports suspension and reprogramming of specified programs, not a permanent stop to every form of aid.
